common_name: Klaus Jelitto Stokes' Aster (Large-Flowered Blue Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in full sun and lean, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; good winter drainage is essential to prevent crown rot.

directions: Klaus Jelitto is named for the German seedsman and is grown for producing some of the largest flower heads of any Stokes' aster cultivar, frequently 5 inches or more across, in a soft powder-blue to lavender-blue that holds its color well through the heat of summer. The compact, low-mounding habit keeps the big blooms from flopping and makes this selection well suited to the front of a sunny border or a cutting garden. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil, since rich or soggy ground leads to weak growth and rot, and deadhead spent flower heads to prolong the early-summer-to-fall bloom season. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep flowering vigorous.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in full sun and well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; avoid wet winter sites.

directions: Silver Moon is a white-flowered selection of the Southeastern native Stokes' aster, opening icy-white, fringed, cornflower-like blooms 3 to 4 inches across with a pale center from early summer into fall. It pairs the same heat and humidity tolerance and drought resistance of the species with a clean, cooling flower color that brightens plantings of blue and purple perennials. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, and deadhead regularly to keep the long bloom season going. Clumps are slow to spread and benefit from division every three to four years to renew vigor.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
Mt. Cuba Center Stokesia trial notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in full sun and well-drained, sandy or loamy soil for the best flower color and longevity.

directions: Purple Parasols is a Stokes' aster selection prized for its shifting flower color: fringed blooms open a pale, silvery lavender and deepen over several days to a rich violet-purple, so a single plant in full flush displays both shades at once for an unusually two-toned effect. Flowering runs from early summer into fall on sturdy, well-branched stems that hold up without staking. As with other Stokesia, good drainage is essential — plant in lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun and avoid wet winter ground, which quickly rots the crown. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain a full, floriferous habit.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; pinch or shear stems by half in late spring to encourage a bushier, sturdier habit.

directions: Blue Star is the most widely sold selection of Japanese aster, distinguished from the plain species by semi-double to double flowers with a quilted, pompon-like pale lavender-blue center surrounded by a fringe of short ray petals — a distinctly different, more refined look than a typical single-flowered aster. It shares the species' outstanding resistance to powdery mildew and its remarkably long bloom season, flowering from midsummer well into fall without the disease trouble that afflicts many native asters. Grow in evenly moist, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full sun; plants stay more compact and need less staking with a spring pinch. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep clumps vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Hortensis Double Japanese Aster (Double White-Flowered Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full sun; shear lightly after the first flush to tidy the plant and extend bloom.

directions: Hortensis is a rhizomatous, clump-forming Japanese aster selection bearing small, semi-double, button-like flowers that open pale lilac in bud and fade to white, produced in loose sprays above finely toothed, dark-green foliage from late spring through summer, with a reliable rebloom into fall if lightly sheared after the first flush. Its tidy, self-supporting habit and tolerance of part shade make it useful as an underused, long-blooming filler for woodland-edge and shaded perennial borders where few other asters perform well. Grow in evenly moist, well-drained soil; unlike many asters it spreads gently by rhizome rather than aggressively, so it rarely needs division for vigor, though clumps can be lifted and split every few years to control spread or propagate more plants.

common_name: E.C. Buxton Golden Marguerite (Pale Primrose-Yellow Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; shear hard after the first flush of bloom to keep growth compact and encourage rebloom.

directions: E.C. Buxton is a long-established golden marguerite selection valued for its softer, pale primrose-yellow daisy flowers, a gentler color than the brassy gold of the species, produced in great profusion over finely cut, aromatic, gray-green foliage from early summer through early fall. Like the species it performs best in poor, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it stays sturdier and blooms longest; rich or damp ground causes lax, floppy growth and shortens its life. Shear the whole plant back by about a third after the first major flush to tidy the habit and push out a strong second round of bloom. Divide every two to three years in spring, since plants are naturally short-lived and benefit from periodic renewal.

common_name: Susanna Mitchell Golden Marguerite (Low-Growing Cream Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; shear after the first flush to maintain a tight, mounded habit.

directions: Susanna Mitchell is a lower-growing, more compact golden marguerite selection than most tinctoria cultivars, forming a dense mound of finely cut, silvery gray-green foliage topped from early summer through early fall with pale cream-yellow daisy flowers that fade to near-white with age. Its shorter habit resists the flopping that can affect taller Anthemis selections, making it a good choice for the front of a lean, sunny border or gravel garden. Grow in poor to average, very well-drained soil in full sun, since fertile or moist conditions promote soft growth and shorten the plant's life. Shear back after the first bloom flush to encourage continued flowering and divide every two to three years to keep clumps vigorous.

common_name: Sauce Hollandaise Golden Marguerite (Creamy Pale Yellow Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; deadhead and shear after the first flush to renew flowering.

directions: Sauce Hollandaise takes its name from its rich, creamy pale-yellow daisy flowers, a color close to E.C. Buxton but on a slightly more compact, densely branched plant with finely cut, aromatic gray-green foliage. Flowers open in great abundance from early summer into early fall, and the muted cream-yellow tone combines easily with blues, purples, and whites in a mixed border. As with other golden marguerite selections, it needs lean, very well-drained soil in full sun to stay sturdy and long-lived; rich or wet ground leads to floppy, short-lived growth. Shear the plant back after its first flush of bloom to keep it compact and encourage rebloom, and divide every two to three years in spring.

common_name: Kelwayi Golden Marguerite (Vigorous Bright Gold Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; shear hard after the first flush, as this vigorous selection benefits most from renewal pruning.

directions: Kelwayi is an old, vigorous golden marguerite selection that keeps the bright, saturated golden-yellow flower color of the wild species while offering a fuller, more floriferous habit over finely divided, aromatic foliage. It is taller and more robust than paler selections like E.C. Buxton, making it a good choice where a strong block of true gold is wanted in the summer border. Grow in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun, since rich or damp soil causes lush but weak, sprawling growth. Shear the plant hard after its first main bloom flush to keep it from becoming leggy and to push out a strong second round of flowers, and divide every two to three years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Sow seeds in early spring, or plant divisions, in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; a top-dressing of grit around the crown helps prevent rot in wet winters.

directions: Juniper-leaf thrift is a tight, slow-growing cushion-forming species from the mountains of Spain, much smaller and more compact than common sea thrift, with dense mounds of short, needle-like, gray-green leaves that resemble a miniature juniper. In late spring it is studded with rounded pink to rose flower heads carried on stems so short they sit almost directly on the foliage cushion, giving the impression the whole plant is briefly blanketed in bloom. It is a classic choice for troughs, rock gardens, and scree beds, where its need for extremely sharp drainage and lean soil can be met; wet, heavy, or fertile soil quickly leads to rot and loss of the tight habit. Full sun and gritty, mineral soil keep the cushion dense and compact for years without division.

common_name: Nifty Thrifty Sea Thrift (Variegated Foliage Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; the variegated foliage colors best in full sun and lean soil, becoming greener in shade or rich ground.

directions: Nifty Thrifty is grown as much for its foliage as its flowers: the narrow, grass-like evergreen leaves are edged in creamy white, giving the tight foliage cushion a bright, variegated look year-round, well before and long after the pink flower balls appear on wiry stems in mid-spring to early summer. The variegation is most crisp and pronounced in full sun and lean, dry soil, and tends to fade toward plain green if the plant is grown in shade or overly rich ground. Like the species it is highly salt- and wind-tolerant and thrives in sharply drained, sandy or gravelly soil, making it a good textural edging plant for coastal gardens, rock gardens, and gravel paths even when out of bloom. Divide every three to four years to keep the cushion tight and the variegation strong.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; deadhead spent stems to prolong bloom and keep the cushion tidy.

directions: Bloodstone is among the deepest-colored sea thrift selections, carrying rounded flower heads in an intense crimson-red rather than the more common rose-pink of the species, held on wiry stems above a tight cushion of narrow, evergreen, grass-like leaves. The saturated flower color makes it a strong accent in edging or rock garden plantings, especially paired with silver or gray foliage companions. It shares the species' toughness — excellent salt spray and wind tolerance, and reliable performance in lean, sharply drained soil where richer or wetter conditions would cause rot. Deadhead through the bloom period to extend flowering from mid-spring into early summer, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain a dense habit and strong color.
